Christ and the Samaritan Woman

Icons

Scriptural scenes

Christ and the Samaritan Woman

Woman at the Well · Christ and Photini

What is depictedHistory and traditionPublished explanationSources

Scripture

John 4:7–15

King James Version · Scripture previews

Emmanuel Tzanes’s composition shows Christ and the Samaritan woman on opposite sides of a well. Smaller scenes unfold in the landscape above the main encounter.

[1] Displayed work;file-level title,description,date and visual identification

What is depicted

The woman carries a vessel while Christ sits beside the well and addresses her. The built well, landscape and surrounding episodes locate the dialogue in a narrative setting. The artist’s rich garments and developed architecture are features of this particular historical composition.

[1] Displayed work;file-level title,description,date and visual identification

History and tradition

The image catalogue attributes the work to Emmanuel Tzanes, a Cretan painter. It is reused here from the exact identified Saint Photini asset, with unchanged bytes and attribution. The named icon connects the woman’s later ecclesiastical commemoration with the encounter narrated in John4; the biblical passage itself calls her a Samaritan woman.

[1] Displayed work;file-level title,description,date and visual identification

Published explanation

There cometh a woman of Samaria to draw water: Jesus saith unto her, Give me to drink.

(For his disciples were gone away unto the city to buy meat.)

Then saith the woman of Samaria unto him, How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.

Jesus answered and said unto her, If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water.

The woman saith unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep: from whence then hast thou that living water?

Art thou greater than our father Jacob, which gave us the well, and drank thereof himself, and his children, and his cattle?

Jesus answered and said unto her, Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again:

But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.

The woman saith unto him, Sir, give me this water, that I thirst not, neither come hither to draw.

Canonical scriptural narrative in the identified historical English edition; later biographical traditions are separately attributed.

[2] John 4:7–15
